name: Silk pillowcase

image.caption: mulberry silk pillowcases silk pillowcase wrinkles

lead: A silk pillowcase is a pillow cover made from smooth, tightly woven silk, usually mulberry silk. People switch to it for smoother hair, less breakage and frizz, and fewer sleep creases on the face when they wake.

A smoother surface lowers friction between hair, skin and fabric as you move in sleep, which could reduce abrasion and creasing. It also absorbs less moisture and product than cotton. Friction figures come mainly from sellers' own tests, and no independent trial of hair or skin outcomes was found.

paras: It simply replaces the regular pillowcase and is used every night, often alongside a hair and skin routine. Washing it regularly is described as mattering for acne-prone skin. Any difference is noticed over weeks of nightly use.
Little risk beyond cost and care requirements. Dermatologists quoted in media say a pillowcase cannot reverse existing damage, and that washing frequency may matter more for acne than the fiber.

chain: Less hair breakage and sleep creases
Smoother hair and fewer face lines on waking
angle.text: Users switch to silk pillowcases to reduce frizz, hair breakage and sleep creases, and some link it to calmer skin. Lower friction than cotton means less rubbing on hair and face overnight, so you wake with smoother hair and fewer pillow lines. Sellers cite friction tests; independent trials have not been found.

lead: A silk pillowcase is a pillow cover made from silk, a natural protein fiber composed mainly of fibroin with a smaller coating of sericin and most commonly obtained from the cocoons of the mulberry silkworm Bombyx mori.[1] It is used in hair and skin care as a smooth alternative to cotton, with the aim of less overnight friction, so less frizz, fewer tangles and breakage, and fewer sleep creases on the face.

Wikipedia describes silk as soft and smooth without being slippery, with flat fiber surfaces that give a sheen.[1] Silk has a long documented history as a textile, beginning in Neolithic China, and a separate history as a biomaterial used in surgical sutures.[1][2] The specific claims made for silk bedding rest largely on mechanism and user experience; no published clinical trial of silk pillowcases on hair or skin outcomes was found.
On looksmax.org the idea has been promoted for years as a cheap hair-and-skin method, and a T Nation member reported that a silk pillowcase given as a hair gift was well received.[3][4]
infobox: Less friction on hair and skin during sleep

paras: Silk fibers from B. mori have a triangular cross-section with rounded corners and flat surfaces that reflect light at many angles, which gives the fabric a natural sheen.[1] Fibroin makes up roughly three quarters of the fiber and sericin most of the remainder; sericin is removed during processing for some uses.[1] Silk is described as smooth and soft without being slippery, and it is a strong natural fiber, though it loses strength when wet.[1]

Silk pillowcases are generally sold in woven forms such as charmeuse or satin-finish silk, often described by a weight measure called momme. Sellers also market silk-like satin made from synthetic fibers as a cheaper alternative; this article concerns real silk.

Silk textiles originated in China; the earliest evidence of silk protein comes from tombs at Jiahu dated to about 8,500 years ago, and the earliest surviving fabric dates to roughly 3630 BC.[1] Production spread along the Silk Road and into Korea, Japan, India and Europe.[1] Silk also became a biomaterial, used as suture material since at least the second century CE and widely studied since the 1990s.[1] Wikipedia notes that wearing silk has sometimes been suggested for atopic dermatitis, but that it is safe for skin without improving symptoms of the condition.[1]
The use of silk pillowcases specifically as a hair and skin product appears to be a modern consumer-market development; the sources reviewed give no reliable date or originator for it.

sections.h: How it is claimed to work
paras: Proponents argue that a smoother surface lowers friction between hair, skin and fabric during movement in sleep, reducing abrasion of hair and creasing of skin, and that silk absorbs less moisture and product than cotton. These are mechanistic arguments made by sellers and users; no controlled study of the claimed effects on sleeping hair or facial skin was located. Friction-reduction figures in marketing typically come from sellers' own testing.

Silk is regarded as safe for skin contact.[1] Practical downsides noted in consumer coverage are cost and care requirements, since silk is a protein fiber that is usually washed gently. Ethical objections exist to sericulture because cocoons are heated or boiled, killing the pupae; organisations such as PETA discourage buying silk, and Mahatma Gandhi criticised its production, promoting wild-silk alternatives.[1]

No studies found. No randomized or controlled human study of silk pillowcases for hair breakage, frizz, sleep wrinkles or acne was identified. Related research concerns silk as a biomaterial and, per Wikipedia, silk clothing in atopic dermatitis, where it was safe but did not improve symptoms.[1]

A looksmax.org thread titled as a method to buy a satin or silk pillowcase and sheets says skin and hair will benefit, especially for people with poor hair and skin. Replies are light-hearted, with one member saying he does not use pillows and another suggesting silk sheets too.[3] A T Nation poster in a confession thread said a silk pillowcase gift for hair was well received.[4]
